title: Tracking FTD quality
summary: How to measure a trading campaign all the way from click to a paid, kept FTD: stage targets, quality by segment, deposit quality and baselines, retention, chargebacks and clawbacks, postbacks and weekly reconciliation. You finish with a quality scorecard and rules that stop you scaling traffic the network will not pay for.

steps.h: The most you can pay per registration
steps.p: Work backwards from the payout. Multiply the payout by the share of registrations that become qualified FTDs, then keep your margin. That gives a target cost per registration you can watch early, while deposits are still arriving.
steps.more: Example: payout $70 per qualified FTD. From the test, 28 of 260 registrations became qualified: 28 ÷ 260 ≈ 10.8%. Margin 25%. $70 × 10.8% × 75% ≈ $5.65 per registration. The test paid $5.38, under the line, so the early signal agrees with the final $50 cost per qualified FTD against a $52.50 target ($70 × 75%). This early line is only as good as the rate behind it: if a new source qualifies at half the rate, its real line is half as high.

steps.h: Which event should the ad platform optimise for?
steps.p: Shallow events give the platform lots of data but attract people who never deposit. Deep events attract better users but there are fewer of them, so delivery can struggle. The usual answer is the deepest event you get often enough.
steps.more: Meta has described needing roughly 50 optimisation events per ad set per week to leave the learning phase. We are not certain this figure is current; check Meta's Help Center. If your deepest event is far below that, optimise one stage shallower but keep judging every ad set on network-confirmed qualified FTDs.

steps.p: Module 1 showed how to find drop-off in the journey. This lesson finds it inside your audience. A campaign at target CPA can contain one segment at twice the target and another well under it. Until you split the results, you are paying for both.

steps.h: How much data before you trust a segment?
steps.p: Small segments swing wildly. Use the same threshold as the CPA kill rule: judge a segment only after it has spent at least 3 × target CPA. Below that, keep watching.
steps.more: Example: target $55. 3 × $55 = $165. A placement that has spent $90 with 0 qualified FTDs is not yet proof of anything, even though it looks bad. A placement that has spent $400 with 3 qualified FTDs ($133 each) has enough spend to act on: it is above the kill line, the lower of 1.5 × $55 = $82.50 and break-even.

Look at the equation: three, times target C P A, equals the minimum spend per segment. With a fifty five dollar target, that's one hundred and sixty five dollars. A placement that spent ninety dollars with zero qualified F T Ds isn't proof yet. One that spent four hundred with three qualified has enough spend to act on. Below the line, keep watching.

steps.h: Why the baseline decides your margin
steps.p: Module 1 covered the baseline and effective payout. At this level, the gap between FTDs and qualified FTDs is where most of your margin is won or lost. Two sources with the same cost per FTD can differ by half on what you are paid.

d.s: The qualification rate is a source's real quality score.

steps.say: Module one covered the baseline and effective payout. At this level, the gap between F T Ds, first-time deposits, and qualified F T Ds is where most of your margin is won or lost. Two sources with the same cost per F T D can differ by half on what you're actually paid. Same F T Ds, different pay. The qualification rate is a source's real quality score.

Geo, meaning resident in an allowed country. And not reversed, with no chargeback or refund in the window. Read the exact words in your deal, and ask for anything vague in writing.

steps.h: What a raw FTD is really worth
steps.p: Multiply the payout by the share of FTDs that qualify. This is the number to bid against when you see a raw FTD in your tracker, long before the network confirms it.
steps.more: Example: 24 of 50 FTDs meet the $100 minimum, which is 48%. $70 × 48% = $33.60. If the trading condition removes a few more, the real figure is lower still. Use your own historic rate per source and geo, recalculated each month.

steps.say: So what's a raw F T D really worth? Multiply the payout by the share of F T Ds that qualify. Look at the equation: a seventy dollar payout, times forty eight percent qualifying, equals thirty three dollars sixty per raw F T D. That's the number to bid against when you see a raw F T D in your tracker, long before the network confirms it. If the trading condition removes a few more, the real figure is lower. Use your own rate per source and geo, recalculated monthly.

steps.h: Why paid is not the same as kept
steps.p: A qualified FTD can still be taken back. Card disputes, refunds, fraud flags and duplicate accounts can all reverse a payout weeks or months later. If you spend every dollar the network pays you, a clawback can arrive when your bank balance is empty.

d.s: Plan cash and targets for what you keep, not what you were paid.

steps.say: A qualified F T D, first-time deposit, can still be taken back. Card disputes, refunds, fraud flags and duplicate accounts can all reverse a payout, weeks or months later. If you spend every dollar the network pays you, a clawback can arrive when your bank balance is empty. A payout can be reversed. So plan cash and targets for what you keep, not what you were paid.

steps.p: Networks use these words in their terms and statements. Read how your network defines each one, because the details decide how much you keep and when.
d: Hold period|days before a conversion is approved for payout
Reserve|share of earnings kept back for a time
Chargeback|a card payment reversed after a dispute
Clawback|network deducts an earlier payout
Fraud flag|conversion rejected as fake or duplicate
Net terms|how long after month end you are paid
steps.say: Here are the words you need. Hold period: days before a conversion is approved for payout. Reserve: a share of earnings kept back for a time. Chargeback: a card payment reversed after a dispute. Clawback: the network deducts an earlier payout. Fraud flag: a conversion rejected as fake or duplicate. And net terms: how long after month end you're paid. Read how your own network defines each one, because the details decide how much you keep, and when.

steps.p: A typical order of events. Timings are rough and vary by network and payment method; card dispute windows can run for months. Ask your network for its exact hold, reserve and clawback terms in writing.
d: Day 0: FTD
Days 7–30: baseline check
Month end + net terms: paid
Months later: dispute window closes
steps.say: Here's the life of one payout, in a typical order. Day zero, the F T D. Days seven to thirty, the baseline check. Month end plus net terms, you're paid. And months later, the dispute window closes. Timings are rough and vary by network and payment method. Card dispute windows can run for months. Ask your network for its exact hold, reserve and clawback terms, in writing.

steps.p: Example: 100 qualified FTDs at $60. The network keeps a 10% reserve for 90 days. Later, 4 FTDs are charged back and clawed from the reserve. The rest of the reserve is released.

steps.p: If a share of your FTDs is reversed later, each one is really worth less. Reduce the payout by your clawback rate before you work out your target CPA.
steps.more: Example: $60 × 0.96 = $57.60. With a 25% margin, the target becomes $57.60 × 0.75 = $43.20 instead of $45. Small difference per FTD, but on 100 FTDs a month it is $180 of margin you would otherwise think you had. Use your own clawback rate per source, from at least a few months of statements.

steps.h: Why CPA alone is not enough
steps.p: Two ad sets can show the same cost per qualified FTD while one brings users who stay and the other brings users who leave or get reversed. Networks see the difference and cut caps, lower payouts or drop affiliates whose traffic is weak. A scorecard shows you what they see, before they act.

d.b: See your traffic the way the network sees it
d.s: One page, every source, every week.

steps.say: Two ad sets can show the same cost per qualified F T D, first-time deposit, while one brings users who stay, and the other brings users who leave or get reversed. Networks see that difference, and they cut caps, lower payouts or drop affiliates whose traffic is weak. A scorecard shows you what they see, before they act. One page, every source, every week.

steps.p: Six numbers per source or ad set, once a week. Each one points to a different part of the chain, so a drop tells you where to look.
steps.say: Here are the six scorecard metrics, once a week per source or ad set. Registration to K Y C approved, know your customer: approved divided by registrations. K Y C to F T D: F T Ds divided by approved. F T D to qualified: qualified divided by F T Ds. Thirty-day active: active at day thirty divided by qualified. Clawback rate: reversed divided by qualified. And cost per qualified: spend divided by qualified. Each one points to a different part of the chain, so a drop tells you where to look.

steps.p: Take clawbacks into the cost. Divide spend by the qualified FTDs you expect to keep. This is the number that compares sources fairly once you have a few months of data.
steps.more: Example: $1,500 spend, 30 qualified FTDs, 5% clawback rate. 30 × 0.95 = 28.5 kept. $1,500 ÷ 28.5 ≈ $52.63. Plain CPA is $1,500 ÷ 30 = $50. A source with a 15% clawback rate at the same spend and count would be $1,500 ÷ 25.5 ≈ $58.82.
d: Spend
(Qualified × (1 − clawback rate))
Quality-adjusted CPA
steps.say: Here's the quality-adjusted C P A, cost per acquisition. It takes clawbacks into the cost. Look at the equation: spend, divided by qualified F T Ds times one minus the clawback rate. For example, one thousand five hundred dollars spend, thirty qualified F T Ds and a five percent clawback rate. Twenty eight and a half kept, so about fifty two sixty three, against a plain C P A of fifty. This is the number that compares sources fairly, once you have a few months of data.

steps.h: Worked example: two ad sets, one week
steps.p: Example: both ad sets cost $50 per qualified FTD. The scorecard shows they are not equal. Ad set Y has weak 30-day activity and three times the clawbacks.
steps.more: Example: X: $50 ÷ 0.97 ≈ $51.55. Y: $50 ÷ 0.91 ≈ $54.95. Y is about 7% more expensive once clawbacks count, and its low activity means it will earn far less on any RevShare part of the deal. If you can only scale one, scale X.

They're not equal. If you can only scale one, scale X.
